content.objective: Apply the concepts from this mission to a device you already own. Map the attack surface of your smartphone — identify what an attacker could reach if they compromised it, and classify each risk using the CIA Triad.
requirements: A notepad or notes app to record findings
instructions: Open your smartphone's Settings and navigate to App Permissions (on Android: Settings → Privacy → Permission Manager; on iPhone: Settings → Privacy & Security). Make a list of 5 apps that have access to sensitive capabilities: Camera, Microphone, Location, Contacts, or Storage.

For each app you listed, ask: 'If this app were compromised by an attacker, what could they access?' Think beyond the app itself — consider what data flows through it (messages, calls, locations, photos, stored passwords).

For each app, classify the primary risk using the CIA Triad: C (Confidentiality — private information could be read), I (Integrity — something could be altered without your knowledge), or A (Availability — you could be locked out of something you depend on).

Now think bigger: if your phone were stolen or your Google/Apple account were compromised, what other accounts become accessible? List the three most sensitive things an attacker could reach from your device.

Finally, identify one concrete action you could take today to reduce your phone's attack surface. (Examples: disable a permission you don't need, enable a PIN, enable 'erase after 10 failed attempts', or review which apps have access to your contacts.)
successCriteria: You have identified at least 5 apps on your device with access to sensitive permissions and recorded what each one can access.
You have classified the primary CIA risk (C, I, or A) for at least 3 of those apps and can explain your reasoning.
You have identified at least 3 sensitive things an attacker could access if your device or primary account were compromised.
You have identified and taken (or committed to take) one specific action to reduce your smartphone's attack surface.
content.reflection: Most people have never thought about their phone as an attack surface. But it likely has access to your emails, your bank accounts, your two-factor authentication codes, your calendar, your location history, your contacts, your camera, and your microphone — sometimes simultaneously. If your phone were compromised, how many of the CIA properties would be at risk? What would the attacker's payload be? This is not a hypothetical: mobile device compromise is one of the most common initial access vectors in both targeted attacks and opportunistic financial fraud.
